overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of how to find out whether an AI model is fit for a particular task. You'll be asked about the jagged frontier, the limits of public benchmarks, the parts of a personal test set, and the requirements of a fair comparison.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: In a field experiment with 758 consultants, those using an AI model did better on a set of 18 tasks and were less likely to reach the correct answer on one other task. What does this pattern show?

options.html: The model was weaker than the consultants at all analytical work
options.text: The model was weaker than the consultants at all analytical work
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The model improved results on 18 tasks, some of them analytical. The pattern shows a jagged frontier: the model's ability was uneven across tasks that looked alike.

options.html: The consultants with AI were less skilled than those without it
options.text: The consultants with AI were less skilled than those without it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The consultants were assigned to groups at random, so the groups were alike in skill. The pattern shows a jagged frontier: the model's ability was uneven across tasks that looked alike.

options.html: The model's ability was uneven across tasks that looked alike
options.text: The model's ability was uneven across tasks that looked alike
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! This is the jagged frontier. The same model helped on tasks inside the frontier and hurt on a task outside it, and the tasks didn't look different in difficulty.

options.html: The model's results got worse the longer the consultants used it
options.text: The model's results got worse the longer the consultants used it
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The difference was between kinds of task, not between early and late use. The pattern shows a jagged frontier: the model's ability was uneven across tasks that looked alike.

forms.stemHtml: A model has the highest score on a widely reported benchmark. What does that score tell you?

options.html: How the model did on that benchmark's tasks and rules
options.text: How the model did on that benchmark's tasks and rules
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A benchmark score is a result on a fixed set of tasks under fixed scoring rules. Whether those tasks resemble your work is a separate question.

options.html: How the model will do on the tasks in your own daily work
options.text: How the model will do on the tasks in your own daily work
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A benchmark's tasks, inputs, and standard for a good answer usually differ from yours. The score tells you how the model did on that benchmark's tasks and rules.

options.html: How rarely the model gives a confident answer that is wrong
options.text: How rarely the model gives a confident answer that is wrong
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Scoring that gives nothing for "I don't know" rewards guessing, so a high score can sit alongside confident errors. The score tells you how the model did on that benchmark's tasks and rules.

options.html: How the model compares with others on every kind of task
options.text: How the model compares with others on every kind of task
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A benchmark covers only its own tasks. The score tells you how the model did on that benchmark's tasks and rules.

forms.stemHtml: Which of these are parts of a test case in a personal test set? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The input, such as a set of meeting notes
options.text: The input, such as a set of meeting notes
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Each test case starts with a real input for the task.

options.html: The request you would make about the input
options.text: The request you would make about the input
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The request is worded as you would normally word it.

options.html: A description of what a good result looks like
options.text: A description of what a good result looks like
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Without this part you have a demonstration and no standard for judging it.

options.html: The model's score on a public benchmark
options.text: The model's score on a public benchmark
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A benchmark score describes someone else's tasks. A test case is made up of an input, a request, and a description of a good result.

forms.stemHtml: A teacher wants to test whether an AI assistant gives useful feedback on student-style essays she has written herself. When should she write her success criterion?

options.html: After the first run, once she has seen what the assistant can do
options.text: After the first run, once she has seen what the assistant can do
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Seeing fluent output first tends to bend the standard to fit what came back. The criterion should be written before she runs any test case.

options.html: After all the runs, when she can compare the outputs side by side
options.text: After all the runs, when she can compare the outputs side by side
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. A standard set after the outputs are in tends to fit the outputs. The criterion should be written before she runs any test case.

options.html: Only if two outputs seem equally good and she needs a tiebreaker
options.text: Only if two outputs seem equally good and she needs a tiebreaker
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The criterion is the standard every output is scored against, not a tiebreaker. It should be written before she runs any test case.

options.html: Before she runs any test case, so the standard can't shift
options.text: Before she runs any test case, so the standard can't shift
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! A criterion written in advance holds still. Fluent output reads as competent, and a standard written afterward tends to adjust to it.

forms.stemHtml: You're comparing two assistants on the same five test cases. Which step makes the judging blind?

options.html: Running every test case twice in new conversations
options.text: Running every test case twice in new conversations
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That is a repeated run, which shows whether a result is stable. Blind judging means hiding which assistant wrote each output before you score it.

options.html: Hiding which assistant wrote each output before scoring
options.text: Hiding which assistant wrote each output before scoring
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Blind judging removes the labels so that a preference for one assistant can't affect the verdict.

options.html: Giving both assistants the same prompt, word for word
options.text: Giving both assistants the same prompt, word for word
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Identical prompts keep the conditions the same. Blind judging means hiding which assistant wrote each output before you score it.

options.html: Scoring each output pass or fail and noting each failure
options.text: Scoring each output pass or fail and noting each failure
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. That is scoring against a criterion. Blind judging means hiding which assistant wrote each output before you score it.

title: Testing a model on your own tasks
